text.text: 1 / PROBLEM
The problem
—  Two arms setting a table is easy to film and hard to believe.
—  A demo video does not say whether the result survives a new random seed.
—  It does not say whether the scorer would have fired with the arms held still.
—  It does not say which of the five steps actually happened, or in what order.
A number nobody else can rerun is not a measurement.
So this entry built the measuring instrument first, and reports exactly how much of the task it can do.

text.text: 1 / PROBLEM
What the track asks for
—  Set a dinner table with two SO-101 arms in a MuJoCo simulation.
—  Interpret language and vision, keep multi-step context, adapt as the scene changes.
—  Show optimized inference with OpenVINO on Intel Core Ultra Series 2/3 hardware.
—  Hold up under randomized placement, weights, friction, shapes and lighting, over 10 seeds.
—  Ship a reproducible repository with deterministic setup, evaluation tooling and benchmarks.
This video says which of those five this entry answers, and which it does not.

text.text: 2 / SOLUTION
What is built — the environment

—  envs/dinner_table.py generates the scene as code: two SO-101 arms, a cabinet with a prismatic drawer holding a fork and a spoon, and a plate, a mug and a bottle — nq=48 nu=12 nbody=25 ngeom=133 nmesh=36, five cameras.
—  envs/randomize.py varies geometry, mass ×0.60–1.60, friction ×0.60–1.29, lighting 0.60–0.94, background and placement, per seed.
—  Placements are rejection-sampled so every episode is reachable, non-overlapping and does not block the drawer: a failed episode is a policy failure, not an impossible scene.
—  16/16 structural and physical checks on the scene pass.

text.text: 2 / SOLUTION
What is built — a scorer with a falsifier
The instruction, verbatim from envs/task.py:
Open the top drawer, pick up the fork and the spoon and lay them either side of the place setting, put the plate on the mat, then set the mug down to the right of the plate.
—  Five ordered sub-goals with 45–50 mm placement tolerances and a 25° upright check; sequencing, which arm touched what, and every hand-off are recorded separately.
—  11/11 accept/reject controls on the scorer pass — it is checked in both directions, so it can be wrong in our favour and be caught.
—  The same scorer, the same 10 seeds, the arms held at their home pose: 0/50 sub-goals. That is the falsifier for every number that follows.

text.text: 4 / RESULT
What it does not do
—  Task success is 0/10. The table has never been set.
—  The plate is hooked by its rim and dragged flat, not picked and placed: it is 94–115 mm across against a 101 mm jaw span, so no jaw opening both clears it and closes on it.
—  Object hand-offs: 5, every one of them the mug. The monitor also records a hand-off on 10 seeds for the drawer handle, which is the two arms taking it in turn and is not an object hand-off.
—  There is no learned policy: no VLA, no imitation learning, no language conditioning. The controller is scripted and reads privileged simulator state.
This is the entry's own scorer reporting against the entry. Nothing above is rounded toward us.

text.text: 5 / TECHNOLOGY
Application of technology
—  envs/perception.py is a 520,768-parameter scene-state CNN that regresses the table layout from one overhead frame, trained on 4,000 simulator-rendered images for 80 epochs.
—  Worst-object error 1.32 mm on validation and 1.83 mm on the ten evaluation seeds, against a no-vision baseline of 42.1 mm and shuffled labels at 46.4 mm. 13/13 pipeline controls pass.
—  Exported to OpenVINO 2026.3.1 IR at FP32, FP16 and NNCF INT8. INT8 is 3.9× smaller than FP32 (527,472 against 2,079,264 weight bytes) and costs 2.16 mm of accuracy — 3.976 against 1.812 mm.
—  That cost is reported, not hidden: a control fails if INT8 is ever recorded as no worse than FP32.
The perception model is NOT in the control loop. That is what the VLA criterion asks for, and it is the next thing to build.

text.text: 5 / TECHNOLOGY
No Intel Core Ultra measurement exists here

—  scripts/bench_openvino.py reports single-stream latency, async throughput at the plugin's own optimal request count, the execution precision the plugin actually chose, and task quality in millimetres — 9 device/precision rows.
—  On this host that is AMD EPYC 9654 96-Core Processor: 0.436 ms median latency, 5,220 inferences/s at FP32.
—  The track asks for Intel Core Ultra Series 2/3 with OpenVINO. This machine has none, so the report stamps itself NOT_THE_REQUIRED_MEASUREMENT rather than offering these numbers as Intel ones.
—  The script is committed and runs unchanged on Core Ultra hardware; the IRs it needs are in the repository.
Reporting AMD numbers as Intel numbers would be falsifying a result. The row stays unearned.

text.text: 6 / VALUE
Value
—  The users are teams training manipulation policies for the low-cost open arms this track names, who today report success rates on environments nobody else can rerun.
—  What is offered is the instrument: a seeded, randomized, ordered-sub-goal task with a falsifier attached — cheap enough to run on a laptop and public enough to argue with.
—  The sustainable form of that is a versioned open benchmark with hosted evaluation, so a robotics team can quote a number it can defend.
None of that is built. There are no users and there is no revenue: it is the route, not a claim.

text.text: 7 / ORIGINALITY
What is unusual — and what comes next
—  The benchmark ships its own falsifier: a no-policy control on identical seeds and an unchanged scorer, so the headline 15/50 cannot be an artefact of the measurement.

—  Three failures were diagnosed by measurement rather than guessed: the stationary jaw planned 7.1 mm inside the mug wall, joint-space ramps sweeping the arm through the cabinet (18 of 25 probe waypoints missed by 40–300 mm), and servo saturation at about 0.30 m of reach with no contact anywhere on the arm.
—  Two are closed, and the plate now places on 6 seeds where nothing had ever placed. The third is a property of the robot and remains open.
—  Next: put envs/perception.py inside the control loop, and find a grasp that lifts the plate instead of dragging it.
